lesson.body:
A first-order filter rolls off at 6 dB per octave, which is the same as 20 dB per decade. Each extra order adds another 6 dB per octave, so a second-order filter falls at 12 dB per octave and a fourth-order at 24 dB per octave. The quoted cutoff of a Butterworth high-pass or low-pass is its −3 dB point, and the slope only settles to its full rate about an octave beyond it. A second-order Butterworth high-pass at 100 Hz is about −3 dB at 100 Hz and about −12 dB at 50 Hz. A second-order filter with Q above 0.707 starts to bump up just before the cutoff, which is why some high-pass filters have a 'resonance' control.

For bells, Q = centre frequency ÷ bandwidth, with bandwidth measured between the −3 dB points. In octaves, a 1-octave band is Q ≈ 1.41, a 2-octave band is Q ≈ 0.67 and a 1/3-octave band is Q ≈ 4.32. Higher Q means a narrower band. Manufacturers do not all measure bandwidth the same way on boost and cut, so the same Q number can sound different between two EQs.

Ordinary analogue-style EQs are minimum-phase: changing the level also shifts the phase near the band. A first-order high-pass has 45° of phase shift at its cutoff, a second-order Butterworth 90°, and a fourth-order 180°. Steeper filters also add more group delay around the cutoff, which can soften the attack of a kick or bass if you set a steep high-pass close to the fundamental. Linear-phase EQs avoid phase shift but add latency and can cause pre-ringing before transients.

In practice: on dialogue, a 12 or 18 dB per octave high-pass around 80–100 Hz removes rumble without thinning most voices; on a mix bus, a gentle 6 dB per octave or a shelf is safer. For crossovers and sub splits, Linkwitz-Riley filters are used because each side is −6 dB at the crossover and the two outputs sum flat. For corrective cuts, use a narrow Q to remove a resonance without taking the surrounding tone; for tonal shaping, use a wide Q and small gain changes.
lesson.inPractice: On a dialogue track, sweep a high-pass from 40 Hz upwards at 12 dB per octave and then at 24 dB per octave, and note where each one starts to thin the voice. Then solo a narrow bell at Q 8 with a big boost, find a resonance, and cut it by only 3–4 dB.
keyPoints: Each filter order adds 6 dB per octave (20 dB per decade).
A Butterworth cutoff is the −3 dB point; full slope arrives about an octave later.
Q = centre frequency ÷ bandwidth; 1 octave ≈ Q 1.41, 1/3 octave ≈ Q 4.32.
Minimum-phase filters shift phase: 45° at cutoff for first order, 90° for second, 180° for fourth.
Linkwitz-Riley crossovers are −6 dB per side at the crossover and sum flat.
Narrow Q for surgical cuts, wide Q and small gain for tone.
lesson.mistake: Many people think the cutoff frequency is where a filter 'stops' the sound. At the cutoff a Butterworth filter has only taken off 3 dB; meaningful attenuation starts an octave or more beyond it.
lesson.sayIt: The slope says how fast the filter fades out the frequencies you don't want, and the Q says how wide a slice of the spectrum a boost or cut touches.
lesson.summary: Every EQ band is a filter defined by its type, frequency, gain and either slope (for high- and low-pass filters) or Q (for bells and some shelves). Slope comes from filter order: each order adds 6 dB per octave. Q describes how narrow a band is: centre frequency divided by bandwidth.

terms.def: The number of reactive stages or poles in a filter; each adds 6 dB per octave of slope.
Quality factor: centre frequency divided by the −3 dB bandwidth. Higher Q means a narrower band.
A filter design with the flattest possible passband and a −3 dB cutoff point.
Two cascaded Butterworth filters, −6 dB at the crossover, whose low and high outputs sum flat.
How much a filter delays different frequencies; it rises near the cutoff of steep minimum-phase filters.
A filter that boosts or cuts everything above or below a frequency by a set amount.

lesson.title: Filter slopes and Q: what an EQ band really does

questions.explain: One octave below the cutoff, a second-order Butterworth is about 12.3 dB down. The trap is thinking the slope starts at the cutoff with 0 dB loss; the cutoff itself is already −3 dB.
questions.q: A second-order (12 dB/octave) Butterworth high-pass filter is set to 100 Hz. Roughly how much does it attenuate a 50 Hz tone?

questions.explain: Q = √(2^N) / (2^N − 1). For N = 1 octave that is √2 / 1 ≈ 1.41. Q 4.32 is a third of an octave, and Q 0.67 would be two octaves.
questions.q: A bell EQ band is set to exactly one octave of bandwidth between its −3 dB points. What is its Q?

questions.explain: A quarter note at 120 BPM is 60,000 ÷ 120 = 500 ms, so an eighth is 250 ms and a dotted eighth is 1.5 × 250 = 375 ms. 333 ms would be a quarter-note triplet.
questions.q: A song runs at 120 BPM. What delay time gives a dotted-eighth-note echo?

questions.explain: Linkwitz-Riley filters are two Butterworths in series, so each side is −6 dB at the crossover; the outputs are in phase and add back to 0 dB. A Butterworth crossover's −3 dB points would give a bump when summed in phase.
options: −3 dB each, so the in-phase sum is +3 dB at crossover
−6 dB each, so the in-phase outputs sum flat
0 dB each, so the sum is +6 dB
−12 dB each, leaving a 6 dB dip
questions.q: In a Linkwitz-Riley crossover, what is the level of each output at the crossover frequency, and how do they sum?

questions.explain: A Butterworth filter has 45° of phase shift per order at its cutoff, so a second-order Butterworth is at 90° and a fourth-order at 180°. Steeper filters shift phase more, which is why steep high-passes near a fundamental can change the attack.
questions.q: Comparing minimum-phase Butterworth high-pass filters, how much phase shift does each have at its cutoff frequency?

questions.explain: Normalisation applies a gain offset equal to the difference: −14 − (−8) = −6 dB. The louder master gains no loudness advantage and keeps whatever dynamics it lost to limiting.
options: It is turned down by about 6 dB
It is turned up by about 6 dB
It is turned down by 14 dB
questions.q: A master measures −8 LUFS integrated. A streaming service normalises playback to −14 LUFS. What happens on playback?

questions.explain: Each filter order adds 6 dB per octave, so a first-order filter falls at 6 dB per octave (20 dB per decade). 12 and 24 dB per octave are second and fourth order.
questions.q: What is the slope of a first-order filter?

questions.explain: XY places the capsules at the same point, so the stereo image comes only from level differences. ORTF spaces cardioids 17 cm apart at 110°, and AB and the Decca tree use spaced omnis.
questions.q: Which stereo technique uses two coincident cardioid capsules angled roughly 90° apart with no spacing between them?

questions.explain: Wavelength = speed of sound ÷ frequency. The speed stays the same in the same air, so doubling the frequency halves the wavelength.
questions.q: If the frequency of a sound doubles, what happens to its wavelength in the same air?
